title: Digestive System

toc.title: 5.1 The alimentary canal and the digestive glands

html:
The digestive system carries 2 of the 40 Zoology questions.

The paper asks it in two ways: a name-and-number question (which cells secrete HCl, which enzyme needs enterokinase, the pH of pancreatic juice, the dental formula) and a route question (where is a nutrient absorbed, and into which vessel does it go).

Almost every mark sits in the enzyme table, the gland table and the absorption routes.

The traps are few but they are asked every year: bile has no enzymes, pepsin works only in acid and trypsin only in alkali, and most absorption happens in the ileum, not the stomach.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • The order of the canal and the epithelium of each segment: stratified squamous (mouth, oesophagus, anal canal), simple columnar (stomach, intestine), and the special cells inside it (parietal, chief, goblet, Paneth, enteroendocrine).
  • The four secretions and their volumes: saliva 1–1.5 L, gastric juice 2–3 L, bile 0.5–1 L, pancreatic juice 1–1.5 L per day, with their pH values.
  • The enzyme → substrate → product → site → optimum pH table, including enterokinase (trypsinogen → trypsin) and the brush-border enzymes (maltase, sucrase, lactase, peptidases).
  • HCl (five jobs), mucus (protection), bile (emulsification — never an enzyme) and bicarbonate (neutralising chyme).
  • The hormones: gastrin (G cells, pyloric antrum, acid + protein), secretin (S cells, duodenum, acid → bicarbonate), CCK (I cells, fat → bile and pancreatic enzymes).
  • Absorption: monosaccharides and amino acids into blood capillaries → hepatic portal vein → liver; fats as chylomicrons into lacteals → thoracic duct → subclavian vein.
  • The applied trio: peptic ulcer and H. pylori, jaundice (three types), appendicitis.

5.1 The alimentary canal and the digestive glands

The alimentary canal is a single muscular tube about 8–9 m long, open at both ends, from mouth to anus. Its digestive glands — salivary, gastric, intestinal, liver and pancreas — pour their secretions into it.

The liver, pancreas and salivary glands are exocrine here because their ducts open into the canal.

The plan of the canal

Every region of the canal is built on the same four coats, from the lumen outwards:

Coat Tissue Job
Mucosa (mucous membrane) epithelium + lamina propria (loose connective tissue with capillaries and lymphatics) + muscularis mucosae secretion, absorption, a first line of defence
Submucosa loose connective tissue, blood and lymph vessels, Meissner's plexus carries away absorbed food; supplies the mucosa
Muscularis externa inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle, with Auerbach's (myenteric) plexus between them peristalsis and segmentation
Serosa / adventitia mesothelium + connective tissue reduces friction; suspends the gut

The two nerve plexuses together form the enteric nervous system, the "little brain" of the gut; it can run peristalsis on its own, but the parasympathetic (vagus) speeds it up and the sympathetic slows it down.

The mouth (buccal cavity)

  • Lined by stratified squamous non-keratinised epithelium, which resists the abrasion of food.
  • Teeth: an adult has 32 permanent teeth; the dental formula is 2·1·2·3 / 2·1·2·3 = 16 + 16 (incisors, canine, premolars, molars per half jaw). The deciduous (milk) set has 20 teeth, formula 2·1·0·2 / 2·1·0·2. Teeth crush and grind food (mastication), giving the surface area that chemical digestion needs.
  • Tongue: skeletal muscle covered with a mucous membrane; it mixes food, helps swallowing, and carries the taste buds.
  • Saliva moistens the food, dissolves sapid substances so that they can reach the taste buds, and begins starch digestion. The ball of chewed food is the bolus.

The salivary glands are three pairs, and the paper asks which is which:

Gland Position Duct Secretion
Parotid (largest) in front of the ear, below the zygomatic arch Stensen's duct opens beside the upper second molar serous — watery, amylase-rich
Submandibular under the lower jaw Wharton's duct opens under the tongue mixed (serous + mucous); most of the resting saliva
Sublingual (smallest) floor of the mouth ducts of Rivinus mainly mucous

Saliva is 1–1.5 L a day, pH 6.8 (range 6.2–7.4), about 99.5 % water.

It contains salivary amylase (ptyalin), maltase in small amount, the glycoprotein mucin (which becomes mucus), lysozyme (kills bacteria), immunoglobulin A, and the enzyme lingual lipase from the serous glands of the tongue.

Salivary amylase converts starch → maltose (plus dextrins) and works best at pH 6.8; it is stopped by the acid of the stomach.

Saliva does not digest protein or fat to any useful extent

Lingual lipase is trivial in adults. Options such as "saliva digests protein" or "saliva contains pepsin" are wrong. Saliva's protein enzyme is absent; its fat enzyme is negligible.

The pharynx and the oesophagus

The pharynx is the shared passage for food and air; the epiglottis closes the glottis during swallowing so that the bolus enters the oesophagus and not the trachea.

The oesophagus is a muscular tube about 25 cm long passing through the diaphragm at the cardiac sphincter. It is lined by stratified squamous non-keratinised epithelium, has no digestive glands of its own and secretes no enzymes.

Food moves down by peristalsis — a wave of contraction behind the bolus — helped by gravity; the whole trip takes about 5–8 seconds.

The cardiac sphincter stops the acid contents of the stomach from running back; when it is incompetent the result is gastro-oesophageal reflux (heartburn).

The stomach

The stomach is a J-shaped muscular bag holding 1.5–2 L. Its regions are the cardia (around the opening), the fundus (the dome above the opening), the body and the pyloric antrum, which ends at the pyloric sphincter.

The mucosa is folded into gastric pits lined by simple columnar epithelium made of several cell types:

Cell Secretion Function
Surface mucous cells mucus + bicarbonate a 1 mm gel layer that keeps HCl off the wall
Parietal (oxyntic) cells HCl (pH 0.9–1.5 as secreted) and intrinsic factor acid; intrinsic factor is needed to absorb vitamin B₁₂
Chief (zymogenic) cells pepsinogen, rennin (infants), gastric lipase protein and milk digestion
G cells (pyloric antrum) gastrin hormone — stimulates acid secretion
Enterochromaffin-like cells histamine amplifies acid secretion
D cells somatostatin inhibits acid secretion

Gastric juice is 2–3 L a day at pH 1.5–2.5. It contains HCl (about 0.5 %), pepsinogen, rennin in infants, gastric lipase, mucus and intrinsic factor.

HCl is not an enzyme. It does five jobs:

  1. Converts pepsinogen → pepsin (removes part of the molecule).
  2. Gives pepsin its acid optimum (pH 1.5–2).
  3. Kills most bacteria swallowed with food — a chemical barrier.
  4. Denatures dietary protein, unfolding it so that enzymes can reach the peptide bonds.
  5. Stimulates the release of secretin and CCK when the acid chyme reaches the duodenum, and helps absorb a little calcium and iron.

Pepsin is the only proteolytic enzyme of the stomach. Secreted as inactive pepsinogen, it is switched on by HCl and then activates more pepsinogen (autocatalysis).

It breaks proteins down to peptones and polypeptides — never to amino acids.

Rennin (chymosin) is present in the stomach of infants; it curdles milk by converting casein → calcium paracaseinate, so that the milk stays long enough to be digested. Adults have little rennin and curdle milk with pepsin instead.

The stomach produces chyme — a soupy, acidic mixture — and passes it into the duodenum in squirts through the pyloric sphincter. Water, alcohol, some salts and a few drugs (aspirin) are absorbed here, but almost no food.

The stomach absorbs very little

A favourite wrong option is "most absorption occurs in the stomach". The stomach absorbs water, alcohol and some drugs only. Over 90 % of the absorption of the products of digestion happens in the small intestine, mainly the ileum.

The small intestine

The small intestine is about 6–7 m long and is the organ of digestion and absorption. It has three parts:

Part Length Special features
Duodenum about 25 cm, C-shaped receives the bile duct and the pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla; Brunner's glands in the submucosa secrete alkaline mucus
Jejunum about 2.5 m longest villi, most digestion and absorption per cm
Ileum about 3.5 m Peyer's patches (aggregated lymphoid follicles); the main site of absorption

Its wall multiplies the absorptive surface three times over: circular folds (plicae circulares), then villi about 1 mm long, then microvilli (the brush border) on every columnar cell. The total area becomes about 200 m², roughly a tennis court.

The epithelium is simple columnar with goblet cells (mucus) and, at the base of the glands, Paneth cells (antibacterial lysozyme).

Between the villi lie the crypts of Lieberkühn, simple tubular glands that supply new epithelial cells every 3–5 days.

Each villus holds a blind-ended lymph vessel (the lacteal) in its centre, a network of blood capillaries, and smooth muscle that makes it sway.

Intestinal juice (succus entericus) is about 2 L a day, pH 7.8–8.2. It is watery and alkaline, with mucus and the brush-border enzymes.

The enzymes are not really poured into the lumen — they sit in the membrane of the microvilli, so that the last step of digestion happens as the nutrient touches the cell that will absorb it.

The large intestine

The large intestine is about 1.5 m long and about 6 cm wide. It runs caecum → ascending colon → transverse colon → descending colon → sigmoid colon → rectum → anal canal.

Its epithelium is simple columnar with very numerous goblet cells; there are no villi and no digestive enzymes.

  • Caecum: a blind pouch below the ileocaecal junction, with the ileocaecal valve that stops backflow. In man it is small (about 6 cm) and its worm-like extension, the vermiform appendix (8–10 cm), is a vestigial organ — in herbivores the caecum is huge and digests cellulose.
  • Colon: absorbs water and mineral salts (about 1.5 L of water a day) and compacts the residue into faeces. The resident bacteria ferment leftovers and synthesise vitamin K and some B vitamins (biotin, folate, B₁₂), which are absorbed here.
  • Rectum: stores faeces until defaecation; the anal canal is lined by stratified squamous epithelium and guarded by two sphincters, the internal (involuntary, smooth muscle) and the external (voluntary, skeletal muscle).

The liver and the gall bladder

The liver is the largest gland of the body — about 1.5 kg, under the diaphragm on the right. It is built of about a million lobules, each with a central vein and plates of hepatocytes separated by sinusoids lined with Kupffer cells.

It has a double blood supply: the hepatic artery (oxygen) and the hepatic portal vein (nutrients from the gut).

Its functions, in the order the paper asks them:

Function Detail
Bile secretion 0.5–1 L a day; bile salts emulsify fat
Carbohydrate metabolism stores glycogen (glycogenesis), breaks it down (glycogenolysis), makes glucose from amino acids and fat (gluconeogenesis)
Protein metabolism deamination of amino acids, urea formation (ornithine cycle), synthesis of albumin, globulin, prothrombin, fibrinogen
Fat metabolism oxidation of fat, formation of lipoproteins, cholesterol synthesis
Storage glycogen, vitamin A, D, E, K and B₁₂, iron (as ferritin)
Detoxification converts ammonia to urea, destroys drugs and alcohol, conjugates bilirubin
Defence Kupffer cells phagocytose bacteria and old red cells
Haemopoiesis in the fetus; stores iron for it later

Bile is a golden-green, alkaline (pH 7.6–8.6) fluid, 0.5–1 L a day, with no enzymes at all. Its composition:

Component Amount / note Role
Bile salts (sodium glycocholate, taurocholate) the important part emulsify fat; help absorb fatty acids and vitamins A, D, E, K
Bile pigments — bilirubin (yellow) and biliverdin (green) from the breakdown of haemoglobin in the spleen excretion only; give faeces their colour
Cholesterol may crystallise into gallstones excreted
Lecithin, water, bicarbonate solvent, neutraliser

The gall bladder is a pear-shaped sac under the liver. It stores bile and concentrates it 5–10 times by absorbing water.

Cholecystokinin (CCK) from the duodenum makes its smooth muscle contract and the sphincter of Oddi relax, so bile squirts into the duodenum when fatty food arrives.

Bile is not an enzyme and does not digest fat

Bile emulsifies fat — it breaks a large drop into thousands of tiny ones, so that the surface area for lipase rises enormously.

The digestion itself is done by lipase. "Bile contains lipase", "bile digests fat into fatty acids" and "bile is acidic" are all wrong: bile is alkaline and has no enzymes.

The pancreas

The pancreas is a soft, lobulated gland lying behind the stomach, with its head in the curve of the duodenum and its tail touching the spleen. It is heterocrine — both exocrine and endocrine:

  • Exocrine part (about 99 %): acini of serous cells drain into ducts that join to form the main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung), which opens with the bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.
  • Endocrine part: the islets of Langerhans — β cells (insulin), α cells (glucagon), δ cells (somatostatin), PP cells.

Pancreatic juice is 1–1.5 L a day, pH 8.0–8.3, and is the most powerful digestive secretion. It contains:

Enzyme Action
Pancreatic amylase starch → maltose
Trypsin (from trypsinogen) proteins and peptones → peptides
Chymotrypsin (from chymotrypsinogen) proteins → peptides
Carboxypeptidase (from procarboxypeptidase) peptides → amino acids, from the C-terminal end
Pancreatic lipase (steapsin) emulsified fats → fatty acids + glycerol
Ribonuclease and deoxyribonuclease RNA and DNA → nucleotides
Bicarbonate neutralises the acid chyme; brings the duodenal pH to about 8

The three proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens. Trypsinogen is switched on by enterokinase; trypsin then switches on chymotrypsinogen and procarboxypeptidase.

This chain is a safety device: if the enzymes were made active inside the pancreas they would digest it — the cause of acute pancreatitis.

The three zymogen switches

Enterokinase → trypsin → (chymotrypsin + carboxypeptidase). Pepsinogen is switched by HCl; trypsinogen by enterokinase. Never the other way round.

The glands and their secretions — one table

Gland Secretion Volume / day pH Enzymes Hormone that drives it
Salivary (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) saliva 1–1.5 L 6.8 salivary amylase, maltase, lingual lipase parasympathetic reflex (sight, smell, taste of food)
Gastric (parietal, chief, G cells) gastric juice 2–3 L 1.5–2.5 pepsin, rennin, gastric lipase gastrin
Liver bile 0.5–1 L 7.6–8.6 none secretin (volume), CCK (gall bladder contraction)
Pancreas pancreatic juice 1–1.5 L 8.0–8.3 amylase, trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase, lipase, nucleases secretin (bicarbonate), CCK (enzymes)
Intestinal (crypts, Brunner's) succus entericus about 2 L 7.8–8.2 maltase, sucrase, lactase, peptidases, enterokinase, intestinal lipase local and vagal reflexes

The enzyme table

Learn this table by rows: the paper rarely asks more than one cell of it, but it can ask any cell.

Enzyme Source Substrate → product Site Optimum pH
Salivary amylase (ptyalin) salivary glands starch → maltose + dextrin mouth 6.8
Gastric lipase chief cells butterfat → fatty acids + glycerol stomach 5–6
Pepsin chief cells (as pepsinogen) proteins → peptones, polypeptides stomach 1.5–2
Rennin (chymosin) chief cells (infants) casein → calcium paracaseinate stomach about 4
Pancreatic amylase pancreas starch → maltose duodenum 7.1–8.2
Trypsin pancreas (as trypsinogen) proteins, peptones → peptides duodenum 7.5–8.5
Chymotrypsin pancreas proteins → peptides duodenum 7.5–8
Carboxypeptidase pancreas peptides → amino acids duodenum 7.5
Pancreatic lipase pancreas emulsified fat → fatty acids + glycerol duodenum 7–8
Nucleases pancreas DNA, RNA → nucleotides duodenum 7.5
Enterokinase intestinal mucosa trypsinogen → trypsin duodenum 7.5
Maltase intestinal brush border maltose → 2 glucose jejunum, ileum 6.5–7
Sucrase (invertase) intestinal brush border sucrose → glucose + fructose jejunum, ileum 6.5
Lactase intestinal brush border lactose → glucose + galactose jejunum, ileum 6
Peptidases (aminopeptidase, dipeptidase) intestinal brush border peptides → amino acids jejunum, ileum 7.5–8
Intestinal lipase intestinal mucosa fats → fatty acids + glycerol ileum 7.5–8

5.2 Physiology of digestion and absorption

Digestion is the breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble ones that can cross the gut wall. It is mechanical (cutting, grinding, churning, emulsifying) and chemical (hydrolysis by enzymes).

Absorption is the passage of the products through the mucosa into blood or lymph. Assimilation is their use by the cells.

Mechanical digestion

Process Where What it does
Mastication (chewing) mouth breaks food up, mixes it with saliva, increases surface area
Swallowing (deglutition) pharynx the bolus is pushed into the oesophagus; the epiglottis guards the airway
Peristalsis all of the canal a wave of contraction behind the bolus moves it forward; it works even against gravity
Segmentation small intestine local rings of contraction chop and mix chyme with the enzymes; it does not move food along
Churning stomach the muscular wall kneads chyme and pushes it through the pylorus
Emulsification duodenum bile salts break fat into droplets of about 1 μm

Chemical digestion of carbohydrates

Step Enzyme Site Product
starch → maltose + dextrin salivary amylase mouth maltose, dextrin
starch → maltose pancreatic amylase duodenum maltose
maltose → 2 glucose maltase brush border glucose
sucrose → glucose + fructose sucrase brush border glucose, fructose
lactose → glucose + galactose lactase brush border glucose, galactose

Cellulose is not digested at all: man has no cellulase, so it passes through as roughage (dietary fibre) — which is not useless, because it gives the colon something to work on and keeps the faeces soft.

Chemical digestion of proteins

Step Enzyme Site Product
protein → peptones, polypeptides pepsin stomach peptones
peptones → peptides trypsin, chymotrypsin duodenum peptides
peptides → amino acids (from the C-terminal end) carboxypeptidase duodenum amino acids
peptides → amino acids (from the N-terminal end) aminopeptidase brush border amino acids
dipeptides → amino acids dipeptidase brush border amino acids

Protein digestion therefore needs three pH environments in turn: acid in the stomach, alkaline in the duodenum, and neutral at the brush border.

This is why a person whose pancreatic duct is blocked loses most protein digestion, and why the faeces of such a patient contain undigested muscle fibres.

Chemical digestion of fats

Fats are not digested in the mouth and hardly at all in the stomach (gastric lipase acts only on already-emulsified butterfat, at pH 5–6). The sequence is:

  1. Emulsification by bile salts in the duodenum — one large drop becomes many small ones, so the surface for lipase increases perhaps a thousandfold.
  2. Hydrolysis by pancreatic lipase: triglyceride → fatty acids + monoglycerides (and some glycerol).
  3. Micelle formation: bile salts gather round the fatty acids and monoglycerides and make water-soluble micelles about 5 nm across, which carry them to the brush border.
  4. Absorption by simple diffusion into the epithelial cell.

Chemical digestion of nucleic acids

Pancreatic ribonuclease and deoxyribonuclease split RNA and DNA into nucleotides; intestinal nucleosidases and phosphatases complete the job to pentose sugar, phosphate and nitrogenous bases.

The parts played by HCl, mucus, bile and enterokinase

Substance Secreted by Part played What it is NOT
HCl parietal cells activates pepsinogen, gives pepsin its acid pH, kills bacteria, denatures protein, triggers secretin/CCK not an enzyme; it digests nothing itself
Mucus mucous cells of the whole canal a viscous glycoprotein gel that lubricates and, with bicarbonate, keeps a pH of about 7 at the cell surface; protects against acid, pepsin and mechanical injury not a digestive juice
Bile liver, stored in gall bladder emulsifies fat; forms micelles; helps absorb vitamins A, D, E, K; neutralises acid chyme; excretes bilirubin and cholesterol no enzymes
Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) duodenal mucosa converts trypsinogen → trypsin, the master switch of pancreatic proteolysis not a digestive enzyme of food; it activates an enzyme
Bicarbonate pancreas, Brunner's glands, bile neutralises acid chyme, raises duodenal pH to about 8 not an enzyme

The stomach wall survives its own acid by a mucosal barrier: a thick mucus layer, bicarbonate trapped in it, tight junctions between the surface cells so that acid cannot leak between them, and a brisk blood flow that carries away any H⁺ that gets through.

Prostaglandins maintain this barrier — which is why aspirin and other NSAIDs, which block prostaglandin synthesis, cause ulcers.

The hormones of digestion

Hormone Secreted by Stimulus Action
Gastrin G cells of the pyloric antrum food in the stomach — especially protein and distension; vagal stimulation stimulates parietal cells to secrete HCl and chief cells to secrete pepsinogen; thickens the gastric mucosa
Secretin S cells of the duodenum acid chyme (pH below about 4.5) entering the duodenum stimulates the pancreas to pour bicarbonate-rich juice; stimulates the liver to secrete bile; slows gastric emptying
CCK (cholecystokinin) I cells of the duodenum and jejunum fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum gall bladder contraction and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi; pancreatic enzyme secretion; slows gastric emptying; causes a feeling of fullness
Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) duodenal K cells glucose, fat inhibits gastric secretion and motility; stimulates insulin
Motilin, somatostatin gut — motility; inhibition

The order to remember: acid → secretin → bicarbonate; fat → CCK → bile and enzymes; food in the stomach → gastrin → acid.

Secretin and CCK are not "the other way round"

Secretin answers acid and makes the pancreas secrete bicarbonate (it has almost no effect on enzymes). CCK answers fat and makes the gall bladder contract. A stem that says "CCK stimulates bicarbonate secretion" is testing exactly this swap.

Absorption

Absorption happens mostly in the small intestine — about 90 % of it, and most of that in the ileum, whose villi are numerous and whose transit is slow.

The duodenum absorbs iron and calcium; the jejunum absorbs most of the monosaccharides and amino acids; the ileum absorbs vitamin B₁₂ (with intrinsic factor), bile salts and the rest; the colon absorbs water, sodium and chloride.

Nutrient Absorbed as Site Mechanism Route
Carbohydrates monosaccharides — glucose, galactose, fructose jejunum, ileum glucose and galactose by secondary active transport with Na⁺ (SGLT-1); fructose by facilitated diffusion (GLUT-5) blood capillary → hepatic portal vein → liver
Proteins amino acids, di- and tripeptides jejunum, ileum Na⁺-dependent co-transport (active) blood capillary → hepatic portal vein → liver
Fats fatty acids and monoglycerides (as micelles) jejunum, ileum simple diffusion into the epithelial cell, where they are re-esterified to triglyceride and packed with protein into chylomicrons lacteal → lymph → thoracic duct → left subclavian vein
Water water small intestine (about 8 L a day), colon (1.5 L) osmosis, following salts blood capillary
Salts Na⁺, Cl⁻, K⁺, HCO₃⁻ mostly ileum, some colon active transport and exchange blood capillary
Iron Fe²⁺ duodenum active transport, helped by vitamin C blood → transferrin
Calcium Ca²⁺ duodenum active transport, requires vitamin D (calcitriol) blood
Vitamins A, D, E, K with the fat ileum in micelles lacteal
Vitamin B₁₂ with intrinsic factor ileum receptor-mediated endocytosis blood
Bile salts — ileum active transport (enterohepatic circulation) portal vein → liver

The mechanism of absorption is worth one more line, because it explains the "against the gradient" questions: the epithelial cell keeps its internal Na⁺ low by pumping Na⁺ out into the blood with the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase of its basolateral membrane.

Na⁺ therefore keeps entering the cell from the lumen, and it drags glucose or an amino acid in with it. The energy is spent on the pump, not on the entry step — that is what "secondary active transport" means.

The hepatic portal route

Every capillary in a villus drains into veins that join to form the superior mesenteric vein, which unites with the splenic vein to form the hepatic portal vein.

This vein enters the liver and breaks up again into sinusoids, so the liver sees the absorbed glucose and amino acids before any other organ — the first-pass effect.

The liver stores or converts what is needed and releases the rest into the hepatic veins → inferior vena cava → heart.

Fats take a different road. A chylomicron is far too large to enter a blood capillary, so it enters the lacteal, is carried through lymph nodes to the thoracic duct, and joins the blood at the left subclavian vein — bypassing the liver at first.

Fat does not go straight into the blood

The single most examined absorption fact: fats → lacteals (lymph), everything else water-soluble → blood capillaries → hepatic portal vein. "Fatty acids are absorbed into the capillaries of the villus" is the standard wrong option.

Applied notes: ulcer, jaundice and appendicitis

Peptic ulcer. An ulcer is an open sore where acid and pepsin have eaten through the mucosa. It occurs in the stomach (gastric ulcer) or, more often, the first part of the duodenum (duodenal ulcer).

For decades the cause was thought to be stress and excess acid; in 1982 Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed that most ulcers are caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, which lives in the mucus layer, splits urea with its urease and neutralises acid around itself, and damages the barrier.

The 2005 Nobel Prize followed. Other causes are NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen), smoking, alcohol and severe stress.

Symptoms: burning epigastric pain, worse when hungry in duodenal ulcer and after food in gastric ulcer; complications are bleeding, perforation and obstruction.

Treatment: acid suppression (proton-pump inhibitors), antibiotics against H. pylori, and stopping NSAIDs. The ulcer is not caused by spicy food.

Jaundice. Yellowing of the skin, sclera and mucous membranes when plasma bilirubin rises above about 1 mg/dL (normal 0.3–1.0 mg/dL).

Bilirubin is the yellow pigment made when haemoglobin is broken down in the spleen; the liver conjugates it and passes it into bile, and the gut bacteria turn it into stercobilin, which colours the faeces brown.

Type Cause Plasma bilirubin Urine Faeces
Pre-hepatic (haemolytic) too much haemoglobin broken down — malaria, incompatible transfusion, haemolytic anaemia of the newborn unconjugated rises no bilirubin, excess urobilinogen normal or dark
Hepatic (hepatocellular) liver cells damaged — viral hepatitis, alcohol, cirrhosis both fractions rise bilirubin present pale
Post-hepatic (obstructive) bile duct blocked — gallstone, cancer of the head of the pancreas conjugated rises dark, bilirubin present pale, clay-coloured

The obstructive type is the one to recognise: dark urine, pale stools, yellow skin and itch. In the newborn, physiological jaundice appears in the first week because the immature liver conjugates bilirubin slowly; it is treated with blue light (phototherapy).

Appendicitis. Inflammation of the vermiform appendix, usually because its lumen is blocked by a faecolith or lymphoid swelling.

The classic story is pain that begins around the umbilicus and settles in the right iliac fossa at McBurney's point, with nausea, low fever and tenderness with guarding.

The danger is perforation and peritonitis, so the treatment is appendicectomy. The appendix has no digestive function in man; it is a vestige of the large caecum of herbivores, though it does contain lymphoid tissue.

Worked examples

How much HCl is in the stomach?

Problem. A fed person has 2.0 L of gastric juice at pH 2.0. How many moles and how many grams of HCl does it contain?

Solution. pH = 2.0 means [\mathrm{H^+}] = 10^{-2} mol L⁻¹. Since HCl is a strong acid, it is fully dissociated, so the amount of HCl equals the amount of H⁺:

n = cV = (10^{-2}\ \text{mol L}^{-1})(2.0\ \text{L}) = 0.020\ \text{mol}

m = nM = (0.020)(36.5) = 0.73\ \text{g}

About 0.73 g of pure HCl, which is why the stomach needs a mucus barrier.

How much alkali neutralises that acid?

Problem. The same 0.020 mol of HCl reaches the duodenum. What mass of sodium bicarbonate is needed to neutralise it?

Solution. NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂, so one mole of bicarbonate neutralises one mole of acid. Required = 0.020 mol. M(NaHCO₃) = 23 + 1 + 12 + 3(16) = 84 g mol⁻¹.

m = 0.020 \times 84 = 1.68\ \text{g}

The pancreas secretes far more than this in a day (about 1–1.5 L of juice at pH 8.3), because acid keeps arriving with every meal.

The surface area of the small intestine

Problem. Treat the small intestine as a cylinder of radius 1.5 cm and length 5.0 m. Folds, villi and microvilli multiply its area about 450 times. Find the plain area and the absorptive area.

Solution. Plain area = 2\pi rL = 2\pi(0.015)(5.0) = 0.47\ \text{m}^2.

Absorptive area = 450 \times 0.47 = 2.1 \times 10^2\ \text{m}^2, about 200 m² — the figure the textbooks quote, and roughly a tennis court. A cylinder alone would give less than half a square metre, which is why the folds matter.

Energy from a meal

Problem. A meal contains 250 g carbohydrate, 70 g protein and 60 g fat. Using 4 kcal g⁻¹ for carbohydrate and protein and 9 kcal g⁻¹ for fat, find its energy in kcal and kJ.

Solution. Carbohydrate 250 × 4 = 1000; protein 70 × 4 = 280; fat 60 × 9 = 540. Total = 1820 kcal. In joules, 1820 × 4.184 = 7.6 × 10³ kJ (7.6 MJ).

Reading a digestion question

Three questions settle almost every stem. (1) Which enzyme? — and therefore which pH. (2) Where? — mouth, stomach, duodenum or brush border. (3) Into what? — blood capillary or lacteal.

If the stem mentions bile, the answer is emulsification, never digestion; if it mentions enterokinase, the answer is trypsinogen → trypsin.

Formula and fact sheet

Lengths, volumes and numbers

Fact Value
Alimentary canal 8–9 m
Oesophagus 25 cm
Stomach capacity 1.5–2 L
Small intestine 6–7 m (duodenum 25 cm, jejunum 2.5 m, ileum 3.5 m)
Large intestine 1.5 m
Appendix 8–10 cm, attached to the caecum
Absorptive area of small intestine about 200 m²
Permanent teeth 32 (2·1·2·3 / 2·1·2·3)

Absorption in one line each

  • Monosaccharides and amino acids → blood capillary → hepatic portal vein → liver.
  • Fats → micelles → epithelial cell → chylomicrons → lacteal → thoracic duct → left subclavian vein.
  • Vitamin B₁₂ needs intrinsic factor and is absorbed in the ileum.
  • Iron and calcium are absorbed in the duodenum; calcium needs vitamin D.
  • Water and salts are absorbed in the colon.

Traps

  1. Bile has no enzymes — it emulsifies.
  2. Pepsin only in acid; trypsin only in alkali.
  3. Most absorption is in the ileum, not the stomach.
  4. HCl is not an enzyme.
  5. Fat goes to the lacteal, not the blood capillary.
  6. Enterokinase activates trypsinogen, not pepsinogen.
  7. Secretin → bicarbonate; CCK → bile and enzymes.
  8. The colon has no villi and no enzymes.

Chapter summary

  • The canal is a 8–9 m tube of four coats (mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, serosa); the enteric plexus runs peristalsis, modified by vagus (up) and sympathetic (down).
  • The mouth has 32 permanent teeth, the bolus is made there, and salivary amylase (pH 6.8) starts starch digestion; the three gland pairs are parotid (Stensen's), submandibular (Wharton's) and sublingual (Rivinus).
  • The stomach secretes 2–3 L of juice at pH 1.5–2.5: parietal cells give HCl and intrinsic factor, chief cells pepsinogen, rennin and lipase, G cells gastrin. HCl activates pepsinogen, kills bacteria and denatures protein; pepsin works only at pH 1.5–2 and stops at peptones.
  • The small intestine (duodenum 25 cm, jejunum 2.5 m, ileum 3.5 m) receives bile and pancreatic juice, and its folds, villi and microvilli raise the absorptive area to about 200 m².
  • The liver (1.5 kg, largest gland) makes 0.5–1 L of bile a day at pH 7.6–8.6 with no enzymes; bile salts emulsify fat. The gall bladder stores and concentrates bile and contracts under CCK.
  • Pancreatic juice (1–1.5 L, pH 8.0–8.3) supplies amylase, trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase, lipase, nucleases and bicarbonate. Enterokinase converts trypsinogen to trypsin, which activates the other two zymogens.
  • Hormones: gastrin (food → acid), secretin (acid → bicarbonate), CCK (fat → bile + enzymes).
  • Absorption: monosaccharides and amino acids into blood capillaries → hepatic portal vein → liver; fats as chylomicrons into lacteals → thoracic duct; B₁₂ in the ileum with intrinsic factor; water and salts in the colon.
  • Applied: peptic ulcer is mostly caused by H. pylori; obstructive jaundice gives dark urine and pale stools; appendicitis gives right iliac fossa pain at McBurney's point.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (c) — a fed stomach is at pH 1.5–2.5. 6.8 is saliva, 7.8–8.2 intestinal juice and 8.0–8.3 pancreatic juice.

2. (b) — parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete HCl and intrinsic factor. Chief cells make pepsinogen, G cells gastrin.

3. (a) — enterokinase (enteropeptidase) of the duodenal mucosa is the only activator of trypsinogen; trypsin then activates the other zymogens.

4. (d) — the gall bladder stores bile and concentrates it 5–10 times; the liver makes it.

5. (b) — bile salts lower surface tension and break fat into droplets, raising the area for lipase. Bile has no lipase, so (a) is wrong.

6. (c) — 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, 3 molars per half jaw, 16 + 16 = 32. Option (a) is the deciduous formula.

7. (a) — the liver, about 1.5 kg; the pancreas is a mixed gland but smaller.

8. (d) — parietal cells. Without intrinsic factor, B₁₂ is not absorbed in the ileum and pernicious anaemia follows.

9. (c) — fatty acids are rebuilt into triglycerides and packed as chylomicrons, which are too large for a capillary and enter the lacteal.

10. (b) — secretin, from S cells, when duodenal pH falls below about 4.5; it drives bicarbonate secretion.

11. (d) — G cells of the pyloric antrum. S cells make secretin, I cells cholecystokinin.

12. (a) — CCK contracts the gall bladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi; bicarbonate is secretin's job.

13. (c) — rennin (chymosin) converts casein to calcium paracaseinate. Adults have little of it.

14. (b) — the ileum, the longest part of the small intestine, with the greatest number of villi.

15. (a) — pepsin is a strongly acid protease, optimum pH 1.5–2; it is inactive at neutrality.

16. (d) — haemoglobin is broken down to haem and globin; haem gives biliverdin and bilirubin.

17. (b) — 20 milk teeth (2·1·0·2 per half jaw); the permanent set has 32.

18. (c) — colonic bacteria make vitamin K (and some B vitamins), which is absorbed in the colon.

19. (a) — aggregated lymphoid follicles in the ileum. They are part of the gut's immune defence.

20. (d) — Brunner's glands sit in the submucosa of the duodenum and pour alkaline mucus into it.

21. (b) — 2–3 L a day at pH 1.5–2.5; 1–1.5 L is saliva or pancreatic juice.

22. (c) — Wharton's duct drains the submandibular gland; Stensen's is the parotid, Rivinus the sublingual.

23. (a) — HCl does not split peptide bonds; pepsin does that, and only as far as peptones.

24. (d) — the appendix opens from the caecum, below the ileocaecal junction.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (b) — HCl removes part of the pepsinogen molecule to make pepsin and holds the pH at 1.5–2, where pepsin works. It supplies no energy.

2. (a) — lipase, amylase and the proteases are all in pancreatic juice; without them fat passes out undigested (steatorrhoea).

3. (d) — the mucosal barrier: thick mucus with trapped bicarbonate, tight junctions, and good blood flow. Prostaglandins maintain it, which is why NSAIDs cause ulcers.

4. (c) — emulsification and micelle formation are physical, not chemical, but without them lipase has almost no surface to act on.

5. (a) — the cell spends ATP on the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺ pump, not on the entry step; the Na⁺ gradient does the work.

6. (c) — S cells respond to H⁺; once bicarbonate has raised the pH the stimulus disappears. This is negative feedback.

7. (b) — first-pass delivery: the liver stores, converts or releases what the gut absorbed before the rest of the body sees it.

8. (d) — stercobilin, from bilirubin acted on by gut bacteria, is the brown pigment. No bile in the gut, no colour.

9. (c) — parietal cells are lost with the stomach, so B₁₂ cannot be absorbed in the ileum even if it is eaten.

10. (a) — unabsorbed lactose is a substrate for colonic bacteria; the gas and the osmotic load cause the symptoms.

11. (d) — pancreatic enzymes have optima near pH 8; the acid chyme would otherwise inactivate them.

12. (b) — pepsin is adapted to acid; at neutral pH its shape and charge change and it stops working.

13. (a) — short diffusion distance plus two exit routes, one for water-soluble and one for fat-soluble products.

Group D — Model answers for long questions (10 marks each, for deeper revision)

  1. Describe the human alimentary canal and the digestive glands with their functions. [10]
  2. Describe the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates, proteins and fats in the human body. [10]

Model answer D1: Alimentary canal and digestive glands (10 marks)

Introduction. The human digestive system has the alimentary canal, about 8–9 m long from mouth to anus, and the digestive glands. Digestion is the breaking of large insoluble food molecules into small soluble ones.

Alimentary canal.

  1. Mouth and buccal cavity: the tongue mixes food with saliva. Humans have 32 permanent teeth; the dental formula is I 2/2, C 1/1, PM 2/2, M 3/3 (= 2123/2123 on each side).
  2. Pharynx and oesophagus: the epiglottis closes the windpipe in swallowing. The oesophagus carries food by peristalsis.
  3. Stomach: a J-shaped bag with cardiac, fundic and pyloric regions. Its inner wall has folds (rugae) and gastric glands: chief cells (pepsinogen), parietal cells (HCl and intrinsic factor) and mucous cells.
  4. Small intestine (about 6 m): duodenum (C-shaped, receives bile and pancreatic juice), jejunum and ileum. The inner surface has villi and microvilli that give a huge absorbing area.
  5. Large intestine (about 1.5 m): caecum with the appendix, colon (ascending, transverse, descending), rectum and anus. It absorbs water and salts and forms faeces.

Digestive glands.

Gland Secretion Main function
Salivary (parotid, sub-mandibular, sub-lingual) Saliva with amylase Starch digestion, moistens food
Gastric glands HCl, pepsinogen, mucus Kill germs, digest protein
Liver (largest gland, about 1.5 kg) Bile Emulsifies fats; also stores glycogen, makes urea
Gall bladder Stores bile Releases bile into duodenum
Pancreas Pancreatic juice (amylase, trypsin, lipase) Digests all three food types
Intestinal glands Intestinal juice Final digestion

Role of the liver. Bile salts have no enzyme, but they break fat into tiny droplets and make the medium alkaline for pancreatic enzymes. Bile pigments (bilirubin) give faeces their colour. Blockage of the bile duct causes jaundice.

Conclusion. Each part of the canal and each gland has a specific part in the continuous process of ingestion, digestion, absorption and egestion.

Model answer D2: Digestion and absorption (10 marks)

Introduction. Digestion is mechanical (chewing, churning) and chemical (enzymes). The products are absorbed into blood or lymph, mainly in the small intestine.

Digestion of carbohydrates.

  1. Mouth: salivary amylase (ptyalin) at pH about 6.8 changes starch to maltose.
  2. Duodenum: pancreatic amylase completes the work.
  3. Ileum: maltase, sucrase and lactase make glucose, fructose and galactose.

Digestion of proteins.

  1. Stomach: HCl (pH 1.5–2.0) kills germs and activates pepsinogen to pepsin, which converts proteins to peptones. In infants rennin curdles milk.
  2. Duodenum: trypsin, chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase make smaller peptides.
  3. Ileum: aminopeptidases and dipeptidases make amino acids.

Digestion of fats. Bile salts emulsify the fat. Pancreatic lipase changes it into fatty acids and glycerol (some monoglycerides). Intestinal lipase finishes the work.

Food Enzyme Site End product
Starch Amylase Mouth, duodenum Maltose
Maltose Maltase Ileum Glucose
Protein Pepsin, trypsin Stomach, duodenum Peptides
Peptides Peptidases Ileum Amino acids
Fat Lipase (+ bile) Duodenum Fatty acids, glycerol

Absorption. Most absorption occurs in the villi of the ileum. Each villus has a capillary network and a central lacteal.

Glucose and amino acids enter the capillaries by diffusion and active transport and go through the hepatic portal vein to the liver.

Fatty acids and glycerol form micelles, are rebuilt into chylomicrons in the epithelial cell and enter the lacteals, reaching the blood by the lymph.

The large intestine absorbs water, mineral salts and some vitamins (K and B12 made by bacteria).

Numerical. A meal with 60 g carbohydrate, 20 g protein and 10 g fat gives (60 × 4) + (20 × 4) + (10 × 9) = 240 + 80 + 90 = 410 kcal.

Conclusion. Digestion changes insoluble food into forms that pass through the villi, and the liver then controls what reaches the body.
